lesson.title: The Fine Print on Every Request
lesson.summary: HTTP headers are the name and value metadata lines that ride along with every request and response, written as human readable text rather than fixed binary fields, describing everything from the requested host to how to parse the body.
lesson.body:
Plenty of protocols attach a block of metadata ahead of their actual payload, describing the payload before delivering it. HTTP does exactly that with headers, but where many lower level protocols pack that metadata into fixed binary fields, HTTP headers are ordinary text: one Name: value pair per line, followed by a blank line that marks where the headers end and any body begins. You already saw a few of these in the protocol chapter's example exchange, Host, Content-Type, and Content-Length, without them being named as headers yet.

It helps to think of headers in three rough groups. Request headers describe the client or the request itself, things like Host, which names the specific site being asked for, User-Agent, which identifies the client software, and Authorization, which carries credentials. Response headers describe the server or its response, things like Server, identifying the software handling the request, and Location, used alongside redirect status codes to say where the client should go instead. Representation headers describe the body itself and apply in either direction, things like Content-Type, which tells the receiver how to interpret the bytes that follow, whether as text/html, application/json, or something else, and Content-Length, which states the body's exact size in bytes.

A couple of headers are worth calling out because they do genuinely load bearing work elsewhere in this chapter set. Host is not just informative, it is what makes it possible for a single server to answer for many different domains at the same IP address, and it becomes mandatory in HTTP/1.1, covered in its own chapter shortly. Content-Type is what lets a client correctly parse a response body without guessing, JSON parsed as JSON, HTML rendered as HTML.

Putting several headers together in one real request and response makes the pattern concrete. A client's request might read:
GET /profile HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
User-Agent: ExampleBrowser/1.0
Accept: text/html

Host says which site on this server to ask, User-Agent identifies the requesting software, and Accept tells the server what format the client would prefer back. A matching response might read:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 2450
Cache-Control: max-age=600

Content-Type and Content-Length describe the body that follows, and Cache-Control tells the client, or anything caching on its behalf, that this response can be reused for 600 seconds before it needs to be fetched again, the same TTL like idea seen earlier for DNS, just applied to an HTTP response instead of a DNS record.
